table.text: We recruited 299 participants from Amazon Mechanical Turk using Turk Prime.
Participants completed the experiment in a median time of 2.39 minutes and were compensated $0.25.
No participants were excluded from analyses.
The sample had a mean age of M = 37.32 (SD = 11.87)-with a minimum requirement of 18 years of age. 143 participants were female.
A total of 301 participants (M(age)= 39.0, SD = 11.9) were recruited through Turk Prime for the Studies 2a and 2b, completing the experiment in a median time of 4.72 minutes. 142 were female.
Participants were compensated $0.40.
Participants were thus randomly assigned to two of the twelve total conditions, with half reading and completing the overt scenario first and the other half first assigned to the covert scenario.
As described above, participants were then prompted to answer questions on 9-point Likert scales.

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> We recruited 299 participants from Amazon Mechanical Turk using Turk Prime.

> Participants completed the experiment in a median time of 2.39 minutes and were compensated $0.25.

> No participants were excluded from analyses.

> The sample had a mean age of M = 37.32 (SD = 11.87)-with a minimum requirement of 18 years of age. 143 participants were female.

> A total of 301 participants (M(age)= 39.0, SD = 11.9) were recruited through Turk Prime for the Studies 2a and 2b, completing the experiment in a median time of 4.72 minutes. 142 were female.

> Participants were compensated $0.40.

> Participants were thus randomly assigned to two of the twelve total conditions, with half reading and completing the overt scenario first and the other half first assigned to the covert scenario.

> As described above, participants were then prompted to answer questions on 9-point Likert scales.

> Methods 200 participants (M(age) = 39.3, SD = 11.47) were recruited through Turk Prime for the study, completing the experiment in a median time of 3.38 minutes; 89 were female.

> Methods 194 participants (M(age) = 40.8, SD = 10.5) were recruited through Turk Prime for the study, completing the experiment in a median time of 6.16 minutes; 80 were female.

> After randomization into one of the four conditions, participants completed exactly the same procedure as in the previous study.

> The original self conditions were used because participants were randomly assigned to them; consequently, mixedmodel descriptives differed slightly from those reported in the overt-only analyses.

In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size. For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like: > An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group. For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like: > A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. info.title: The Good, the Bad, and the Vengeful: Evaluations of Standing up for Oneself versus Having Another's Back

text.text: Bystander evaluations are a relatively unexplored area of retaliation, yet they are crucial to the reputations through which people navigate the social world.
Further, though generally deriding harm, people are often forced to contend with it.
By examining how people evaluate retaliationor the choice not to retaliate-on behalf of self, friend, or stranger in various circumstances, we observed several interconnected results.
We found that retaliation was favored when open and visible to offender and onlookers and also commensurate with the original offense and condemned when considered surreptitious and harsh.
In addition, the more retaliation was endorsed, the more highly people rated retaliation for allies (friends) over self-and third-party retaliation.
Conversely, in scenarios where retaliation was regarded more negatively, people judged abstaining from retaliation for oneself and others with greater approval.
Notably, harsh retaliation-while judged negatively-produced both a deterrence effect and even suggested potential for future helping behavior.
In conjunction with these findings, we predicted and found that loyalty is an important component in the mechanism underlying the evaluation of retaliation.
Overall, the current studies suggest that retaliation may be the particular domain of alliesdiffering qualitatively from third-party retaliation-and is not a form of straightforward assistance.
Recruiting from the United States, our studies provide evidence for how Americans construe and respond to retaliation, yet such evaluations may not fully generalize to other cultures.
In addition, our research examined several questions that would benefit from future clarification.
When we investigated proportionality by manipulating transparency and form of retaliation, we did not distinguish their independent effects.
We also compared retaliation with straightforward helping behavior and examined perceptions of deterrence and helpfulness.
Our findings suggest that severe retaliation may discourage future exploitation but at the cost of bystander approval.
Future research could further explore this tradeoff, isolate important contributing factors, and assess the ecological validity of these findings in other contexts.
Consider the simple case of a playground or office bully.
Who does not empathize with and root for the victim who punches back-figuratively or not?
Even uninvolved witnesses sanction and sometimes champion retaliation (e.g., Carlsmith & Robinson, 2002; Fiske & Rai, 2014).
text.formatted: Even uninvolved witnesses sanction and sometimes champion retaliation (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Carlsmith & Robinson, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Fiske & Rai, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Contrast this scenario with a friend who takes up the cause, or even a third party who presumably intervenes out of a general sense of justice.
Standing up for oneself is laudable, but we hypothesized that taking on a bully for someone else would be even more praiseworthy.
Conversely, there are situations in which retaliation is considered undesirable or even detestable (Study 4).
People readily condemn it when they perceive it to be disproportionate, surreptitious, or inordinately harsh (e.g., Studies 2b and 4).
In such circumstances, is acting on behalf of someone else still considered more favorable?

Over the course of five studies, our research provides new evidence that people have predictably different appraisals of these three forms of retaliation: on behalf of oneself, on behalf of an ally, and on behalf of a third-party stranger.
Intriguingly, our results suggest that retaliation may be the particular domain of allies.
We find that retaliation for an ally (i.e., a friend, in our studies) can be extremely praiseworthy, but crucially only when the act of retaliation, itself, is deemed warranted.
When people condone overall retaliation, they tend to find retaliation for a friend more commendable than retaliation for oneself or for a third party.
As one possible explanation for this privileged role of allies, retaliation may be valued as a partial (vs. impartial) behavior.
Indeed, we demonstrate that perceived loyalty is a component in the mechanism regulating the evaluation of retaliation.

Retaliation is pervasive and primordial, existing across modern cultures (e.g., Ericksen & Horton, 1992 , Harinck et al., 2013), in isolated tribes (e.g. Boehm 1987), and even in other species (Clutton-Brock & Parker, 1995; de Waal 1996).
text.formatted: Retaliation is pervasive and primordial, existing across modern cultures (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Ericksen & Horton, 1992</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">, Harinck et al., 2013)</ref>, in isolated tribes (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Boehm 1987)</ref>, and even in other species <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Clutton-Brock & Parker, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">de Waal 1996)</ref>.

text.text: Formally, we define retaliation as the act of inflicting vengeance-some form of harm by imposing cost on an offender-for a perceived transgression against oneself or another.
While prior work often uses different verbiage to refer to various categories of the phenomenon-e.g., "revenge" or "punishment"-we use "retaliation" for the sake of simplicity.

By this broad definition, studies in the lab (e.g., Camerer 2003; Güth et al., 1982) and in the field (e.g., Balafoutas et al., 2014; Mitchell & Ambrose, 2007; Tripp & Bies, 2009) have demonstrated that people engage in retaliation, both for themselves (Brown 1991) and for others (Boyd et al. 2003; Sober & Wilson 1998).
text.formatted: By this broad definition, studies in the lab (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Camerer 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Güth et al., 1982)</ref> and in the field (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Balafoutas et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Mitchell & Ambrose, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Tripp & Bies, 2009)</ref> have demonstrated that people engage in retaliation, both for themselves <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Brown 1991</ref>) and for others <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Boyd et al. 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Sober & Wilson 1998)</ref>.

text.text: Yet retaliation can be perilous.
Retaliators risk harm, reputational loss, or escalating patterns of resentment like feuds (e.g., Elshout et al., 2017; Keysar et al., 2008; Stillwell et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Retaliators risk harm, reputational loss, or escalating patterns of resentment like feuds (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Elshout et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Keysar et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Stillwell et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Further, people generally have a strong aversion to inflicting harm (Cushman et al., 2012; Schein & Gray, 2018).
text.formatted: Further, people generally have a strong aversion to inflicting harm <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Cushman et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Schein & Gray, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: However, retaliation may nonetheless persist for several reasons.

It may deter further offense (e.g., Krasnow et al., 2012 Krasnow et al., , 2016;; McCullough et al., 2013; Nagin, 1998) and also preserve and communicate status and friendship (e.g., Fiske & Rai, 2011).
text.formatted: It may deter further offense (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Krasnow et al., 2012</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Krasnow et al., , 2016;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">McCullough et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Nagin, 1998)</ref> and also preserve and communicate status and friendship (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Fiske & Rai, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, scholars argue that reputational concerns like trustworthiness underlie both retaliation and reciprocity (e.g., Raihani & Bshary, 2015; dos Santos, 2012; Nowak & Sigmund, 2005; Trivers, 1971).
text.formatted: Indeed, scholars argue that reputational concerns like trustworthiness underlie both retaliation and reciprocity (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Raihani & Bshary, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr">dos Santos, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Nowak & Sigmund, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Trivers, 1971)</ref>.

text.text: Given potential costs, people must be shrewd in employing retaliation to avoid negative repercussions.

The age-old "eye for an eye" can thus be construed as both an endorsement of retaliation and an admonition that the severity and nature of retaliation must be carefully calibrated to match and not exceed that of the original offense.

In a legal setting, Carlsmith and colleagues (2002) found that people condone "punishments" for criminals that are deemed to "fit" their offenses (e.g., see also Kundro et al., 2026; Seubert & Böckler, 2025).
text.formatted: In a legal setting, <ref type="bibr">Carlsmith and colleagues (2002)</ref> found that people condone "punishments" for criminals that are deemed to "fit" their offenses (e.g., see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Kundro et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Seubert & Böckler, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, we assert that retaliation must be perceived to be warranted for bystanders to sanction it.
That is, it must be deemed a compatible and proportionate response.
However, retaliation may still be productive if the costs imposed do exceed the costs inflicted by instigating offense-especially if one motivating factor is deterrence of future harm.
Yet, if the offense and the retaliation are incongruent, the retaliator increases the risk of devastating consequences in the form of backlash.
There is scant direct evidence on how people evaluate retaliation on behalf of oneself vs. others, much less for allies, alone.
However, some findings provide insight into how such behaviors might be construed differently.
Further, evidence suggests that retaliation may differ from "help" and may be an altogether separate category of action.
We investigate this possibility most directly in Studies 3 and 4.

Research indicates that people may regard third-party retaliation as trustworthy (e.g., Jordan et al., 2016), concerned with fairness-especially as costliness increases (e.g., Nelissen 2008)-and otherwise prosocial (e.g., Fehr & Gachter, 2002).
text.formatted: Research indicates that people may regard third-party retaliation as trustworthy (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Jordan et al., 2016)</ref>, concerned with fairness-especially as costliness increases (e.g., Nelissen 2008)-and otherwise prosocial (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Fehr & Gachter, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: In one of the few studies to compare punishment for oneself vs. third-party punishment, Chen et al. (2020) demonstrated that people regarded third-party punishers as more impartial.
text.formatted: In one of the few studies to compare punishment for oneself vs. third-party punishment, <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Chen et al. (2020)</ref> demonstrated that people regarded third-party punishers as more impartial.

text.text: Further, "audience effects" indicate that third parties become more punitive in the real or implied presence of observers, while second parties (victims) become less punitive (see Andreoni & Bernheim, 2009; Goeschl & Jarke, 2016; Kurban et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Further, "audience effects" indicate that third parties become more punitive in the real or implied presence of observers, while second parties (victims) become less punitive (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Andreoni & Bernheim, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Goeschl & Jarke, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Kurban et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: These findings are also consistent with people's general disapproval of partiality (e.g., Choshen-Hillel et al., 2018).
text.formatted: These findings are also consistent with people's general disapproval of partiality (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Choshen-Hillel et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The data indicate that retaliators are conscious of the messages they may be conveying to observers (e.g., Gollwitzer & Denzler, 2009; Sarin et al., 2021)-though as our studies suggest, their intentions may not always translate to outsider evaluations.
text.formatted: The data indicate that retaliators are conscious of the messages they may be conveying to observers (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Gollwitzer & Denzler, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Sarin et al., 2021)</ref>-though as our studies suggest, their intentions may not always translate to outsider evaluations.

text.text: Conversely, although retaliating for an ally-as opposed to retaliating on behalf of a stranger-suggests partiality, retaliation may be one realm in which a kind of partiality is not only tolerated but expected and lauded.
Indeed, a study by Lieberman & Linke (2007) found people applied less punishment for offenses committed by kin and allies while still condemning their actions to equal degree.

text.text: In fact, retaliation may do so to even a greater degree than generic prosocial behavior because it involves risk, whereas "straightforward" help does not.
The retaliator advertises herself as a valuable future ally or community member.
Relatedly, choosing not to retaliate on behalf of oneself or one's allies may have very different implications, depending on context.

Forgoing retaliationespecially for an offense against oneself or for an ally-may be considered an indication of strength because it suggests the victim is not threatened and/or has strong allegiances.
However, our studies suggest this is a delicate balance: Retaliate too infrequently, and you are perceived as weak; retaliate too much or aggressively and you are considered insecure or abusive.
Further, when not perceived as warranted, retaliation for others may be construed as favoritism.

If it is the dynamics of the social environment that provokes retaliation and how it is received by others, observer judgments should be especially revealing about the nature, purpose, and mechanism of retaliation.
Likewise, the relationship of the retaliator to the victim should be a prominent consideration.
Through the course of our five studies, we asked the following questions: (1) How does the identity of the agent and his relationship to the victim affect evaluations of retaliation?
(2) In general, when do people regard retaliation positively vs. negatively?
(3) How does the identity of the agent interact with contextual variables like proportionality and transparency (especially Studies 2 and 4)?
More specifically, when is retaliation considered warranted, and what are the effects of this appraisal?
How does loyalty feature in the underlying mechanisms supporting retaliation?
(4) Is retaliation a form of assistance?

(examined in Studies 3 and 4) (5) Do people evaluate choosing to retaliate differently than choosing not to: that is, is abstaining from retaliation considered an active choice or does it simply constitute a lack of action?
STUDY 1:
In Study 1, people read a scenario in which an offender accosts a victim walking in the park and steals his bag.
Several people witness the crime-namely, the victim (self conditions), the victim's ally (friend conditions), and a third-party (stranger conditions).
Later, one of the three-the "agent"-encounters the thief and has an opportunity to retaliate or abstain.
We recruited 299 participants from Amazon Mechanical Turk using Turk Prime.

The intended number was 300 with an even 50/cell but, despite our best effort at randomization and counterbalancing, occasional dropout produced very slight differences in cell sizes (reported below).
This was true for each study.
Participants completed the experiment in a median time of 2.39 minutes and were compensated $0.25.
No participants were excluded from analyses.
The sample had a mean age of M = 37.32 (SD = 11.87)-with a minimum requirement of 18 years of age. 143 participants were female.
Additional demographic details for each study are available upon request.
In the first three studies (Studies 1, 2a, 2b), we manipulated two factors: 3 (Agent: self vs. friend vs. third party) × 2 (Action: retaliation vs. no retaliation) in a between-subjects design.
The last two studies comparing retaliation and help used only friend and third-party conditions (see Studies 3 and 4 for the rationale).
Across our five studies, we systematically varied contextual circumstances (e.g., scene, transparency, and severity of retaliation).
Tests were planned, independent-samples and two-tailed, with 95% confidence intervals (CI), unless Levene's test indicated a violation of the assumption of homogeneity of variance.
Cohen's d served as effect size among the t-tests.

The primary dependent variable was consistently a bipolar rating of praiseworthiness or blameworthiness of the agent, which we interpreted not only as one of approval but also as a sanctioning of the particular actions at hand-i.e., a determination of whether participants considered them warranted.
While many other relevant studies have involved economic games, ours consisted of narratives intended to mimic real-life circumstances.
Based on the prior literature, we had several hypotheses, some of which acquired greater clarity as the studies built on one another.
Hypothesis 1a (Prosociality): People favor retaliation for others over retaliation for oneself.
We hypothesized that people would regard retaliating for others-friend or stranger-more positively than retaliating for oneself.
While people may sympathize and endorse retaliation for oneself as a demonstration of strength and character, retaliation for another is more easily conceptualized as prosocial.
Choosing not to retaliate for oneself may be a demonstration of strength.
We further hypothesized that abstaining from retaliation would at least partially present the inverse pattern.
That is, choosing not to retaliate on one's own behalf would be interpreted as more praiseworthy.

However, beyond simply representing the "opposite" choice from retaliation, we theorized that actively making the deliberate choice not to retaliate for oneself when there was opportunity could be a particular show of magnanimity, strength, or confidence.
While these first two hypotheses may present congruent predictions, we predicted that people might evaluate retaliating and not retaliating to some degree independently.
In these ways, deciding not to retaliate did not always prove to be a simple inversion of retaliating.
In particular, there may be an inflection point after which retaliating for oneself is less praiseworthy.
Retaliation may be the particular sphere of allies.
Even if not exclusively the domain of allies, retaliation on behalf of friends and third parties may be qualitatively distinct.
We hypothesized that both could be evaluated as especially praiseworthy-though for different reasons.

Retaliation for a friend may reflect loyalty but also indicate self-interest (Shaw et al., 2018), whereas third-party retaliation may signal impartiality (e.g., Marshall et al., 2020; McManus et al., 2020).

text.text: As discussed, each participant in Study 1 read a short, hypothetical vignette about a perpetrator committing a transgression in a park.
The vignettes read as follows, depending on condition: [Agent] ultimately decides to let it go and continue walking home.
We include the full scenario text in each respective study to preserve critical nuance and ensure transparency in experimental manipulations.
For clarity-and to align with color-coding used in figures-agent names appear in color (red = self, blue = friend, green = third party).
After reading their respective scenarios, the praiseworthiness measure was presented first of a total of five DVs.
We predicted that retaliation would be rated more favorably when enacted on behalf of others (a friend or stranger) than for oneself.
We also expected the reverse pattern for the no-retaliation conditions: that failing to act for others would be interpreted as less supportive than abstaining on one's own behalf.

However, in this scenario, we also thought it less likely that failing to retaliate would be judged as especially praiseworthy (as in Study 2b, for instance) because outrage on one's own behalf seems justified.
To further test our predictions, in Study 1 we also included four additional variables, presented in counterbalanced order.
All five took the basic format of: "Do you think that [Agent's] actions were [praiseworthy or blameworthy]?

In the case of the "loyalty/disloyalty" question, the phrasing was slightly different so that the measure could be applied to circumstances in which people acted for themselves (i.e., the self-conditions).
The question appeared as follows: "In general life, do you think that [Agent] is a loyal or disloyal friend."
Participants registered their answers on 9-point scales, ranging from "Extremely We were especially interested in the bipolar measure of loyalty/disloyalty.

If the second possibility in Hypothesis 2 regarding partiality for allies is true-that is, retaliating for friends is most praiseworthy-we expected that loyalty would figure in evaluations of praiseworthiness.
In this scenario, we predicted that it might, in fact, interact with or even partially mediate the effect of condition and thus we planned and performed moderation and mediation analyses.
While the other measures were not our primary foci, we expected that retaliating for others (vs. oneself) would be rated higher on these measures.
Though likewise not central to our hypotheses, we included the three secondary measures-morality, heroism, and altruism-to capture broader dimensions of social evaluation.

However, the correlations among the five measures were so apparent that we decided to conduct a principal-component analysis, rather than analyzing them separately (available in Supplemental Materials).
As by far the most dominant, we used Principal Component 1 (PC1) as a DV.

Morality, altruism, and heroism all correlated closely with praiseworthiness and loyalty though, they seemed, once again, to coincide most closely on the non-retaliation side.

Importantly, the correlations for specific conditions between loyalty and praiseworthiness were consistent with one another: One might suppose that loyalty for a friend would be more correlated with praiseworthiness than other conditions, but this was not the case.

The dramatic nature of the scenario may account for the lack of differentiation among the retaliators.

Indeed, this scenario may have qualified less as "retaliation" than as a justice scenario-retrieving a stolen item-with the "shouting" component being too understated to register clearly as retaliation.
Whether or not it constituted unequivocal retaliation, it was extremely well-received.

In accordance with the Prosociality Hypothesis, retaliating for oneself was rated least praiseworthy; as predicted by the Integrity Hypothesis, abstaining from retaliation for oneself rated significantly higher than the friend condition.
In the PCA analyses, retaliation for oneself was significantly less positive than its counterpart conditions and choosing not to retaliate for oneself was more positive.
Retaliating for a friend was rated highest, failing to retaliate for a friend lowest.

Such results add conceptual complexity, especially considering that (1) Participants evaluated retaliation and abstaining partially independently; (2) failing to act for a friend was rated as especially blameworthy (followed by failing a third-party); (3) loyalty exhibited strong main, moderating, and mediating effects.
These findings also argue for one possibility discussed in our Hypothesis 2: that retaliation may be the particular domain of allies.

text.text: Study 2 had several objectives: First, to examine retaliation in isolation; second, to investigate the implications of using two scenarios that are clearly less criminal (relative to the theft) and situated in a more naturalistic, well-established context-an office setting.
foot_0 Finally, we investigated the effects of proportionality and transparency by comparing an "overt" (Study 2a) scenario and a "covert" scenario (Study 2b).
text.formatted: <ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">foot_0</ref> Finally, we investigated the effects of proportionality and transparency by comparing an "overt" (Study 2a) scenario and a "covert" scenario (Study 2b).

text.text: A total of 301 participants (M(age)= 39.0, SD = 11.9) were recruited through Turk Prime for the Studies 2a and 2b, completing the experiment in a median time of 4.72 minutes. 142 were female.
Once again, we had aimed for 300 to produce 50/cell, but due to slight drop-out, the cells were not precisely even (see below).
Participants were compensated $0.40.
None were excluded from analyses.
Study 2a and Study 2b employed the same participants.
As in Study 1, we used a 3 (Agent: self vs. friend vs. third party) × 2 (Action: retaliation vs. no retaliation) design.
However, in this mixed design, each participant read and responded to two vignettes (in counterbalanced order): one "overt" (Study 2a) and one "covert" (Study 2b).
Participants were thus randomly assigned to two of the twelve total conditions, with half reading and completing the overt scenario first and the other half first assigned to the covert scenario.

In each vignette, the agent chose either to retaliate or refrain from doing so on behalf of themselves, a friend, or a relatively unknown coworker-this time in an office setting, where retaliation is known to occur (Bordia et al., 2014; Tripp & Bies, 2009).
text.formatted: In each vignette, the agent chose either to retaliate or refrain from doing so on behalf of themselves, a friend, or a relatively unknown coworker-this time in an office setting, where retaliation is known to occur <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bordia et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Tripp & Bies, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: After each vignette, participants responded to six 9-point Likert scale items, including praiseworthiness and loyalty (our primary DVs).
To bolster these measures, we also included two additional items: how "good or bad" the agent's actions were and how "good or bad a friend" they were perceived to be.
These were highly correlated with praiseworthiness and loyalty, respectively.
The full procedure was then repeated with the second vignette.
The Scenarios (Tables 5 and 6).
text.formatted: The Scenarios (Tables <ref type="table">5</ref> and <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">6</ref>).

text.text: In constructing these two vignettes, we sought to: (1) assess whether results would replicate or diverge from Study 1; and (2) examine reactions to retaliation differing in transparency and proportionality.

In the "overt" scenario (Study 2a), retaliation involved a direct, public confrontation of the offender (i.e., transparent), designed to be congruent with the original offense (i.e., proportional)-or warranted.
In contrast, in the "covert" vignette (Study 2b), retaliation took the form of a private, negative, and unrelated report to a supervisor, without the offender-or any onlookers-present.
We anticipated that the overt response would be more readily perceived as warranted and that the covert response would elicit more misgivings and/or ambivalence.
We were especially interested in testing two predictions derived from our hypotheses.
First, we expected that in the overt scenario, retaliation for a friend would be rated most positively-a prediction that was largely supported by Study 1 findings.

Second, we hypothesized that in the covert scenario, choosing not to retaliate on one's own behalf might be evaluated more positively than retaliating for oneself, potentially reflecting restraint or integrity when retaliation is not clearly deemed justified.
Because of a minor typographical error, self conditions for Study 2a were run again; results did not materially differ.
(See Supplemental Materials for further explanation.)

text.text: Because we expected and observed distinctly different patterns within the two scenarios, we combined them in a mixed regression.

This allowed us to examine how transparency (overt vs. covert retaliation) operates across contexts that differ markedly in proportionality-that is, in the perceived appropriateness of retaliation relative to the offense.

In addition to other aspects of proportionality that differ between the two, transparency is perhaps most salient: It may be an essential dimension of proportionality, insofar as actions must be visible in order to ( 1) exert a strong impact on bystanders and (2) undergo social evaluation by those affected, directly or indirectly.

In the overt scenario, retaliating for a friend was rated significantly more praiseworthy than the other two conditions.
Likewise, failing to retaliate for oneself was judged less blameworthy than for friend or third party.
These patterns are especially notable because people tend to value impartiality in many fairness contexts.
By contrast, the covert scenario reflected greater ambivalence toward retaliation.

One explanation is that in overt contexts, retaliation signals integrity and prosocial commitment, whereas covert retaliation lacks this visibility and imperative of proportionality-i.e., being warranted or normatively sanctioned.

In that context, abstaining from retaliation for oneself was rated more positively than all other five conditions, reinforcing the findings that retaliation and non-retaliation do not always mirror one another.
People evaluate them differently and may regard not retaliating as an active decision, requiring agency.
Notably, the loyalty ratings aligned with the praiseworthiness ratings in both studies.
These results provide support for retaliation as the particular domain of allies-and the corollary possibility that retaliation is a partial mechanism.
When approved, people seem to regard retaliating for a friend as a positive form of partiality-loyalty-rather than a negative onefavoritism.
Further, these characteristics suggest retaliation differs from other examples of assistance if it qualifies as aid at all.
Study 3 examined this possibility by directly comparing an act of retaliation and one of help, focusing only on friend and third-party comparisons.

We predicted that in the helping context, assisting a stranger would be rated as more praiseworthy than helping a friend: As reviewed, people are regarded as having obligations to friends; they may, therefore, believe helping a stranger is more commendable because it goes "beyond" duty to close others.
By contrast, in our studies participants consistently rated retaliating for a friend as more commendable than for a stranger, sometimes significantly but always in magnitude.
We, therefore, predicted opposing patterns: Retaliation would be rated more positively for friends than strangers, whereas help would be rated more positively for strangers than friends.
This contrast provided an additional test of our more speculative second hypothesis: that retaliation is essentially partial, perhaps the particular mandate of allies.

In both cases-retaliation and help-the friend was judged to be more inclined to retaliate for himself, though neither comparison was significant: neither friend (M = 5.80, SD = 2.15, CI [5.19, 6.41]) vs. third-party retaliator (M = 5.33, SD = 2.07, CI [4.73, 5.92]; t(97) = 1.12, p = .266, d = 0.22, CI [-0.17, 0.62]), nor friend (M = 3.81, SD = 1.82, CI [3.30, 4.31]) vs. third-party helper (M = 3.53, SD = 1.89, CI [2.99, 4.07]); t(99) = 0.75, p = .455, d = 0.15, CI [-0.24, 0.54]).

Although positivity results were not significant, they suggested the predicted pattern, with retaliation for a friend rated higher than retaliation for a third party and vice versa for the "help" conditions.
The help conditions, especially, were also close to ceiling, which may have obscured the effects.

Inferred loyalty has consistently differentiated retaliatory conditions from one anothersignaling willingness to defend close others over strangers-whereas extending aid to strangers was indicative of future helpfulness, reinforcing separable processes.

The measures revealed additional asymmetries: Perceptions of retaliation coincided with expectations of future helpfulness (i.e., outside primary domain), but helping did not suggest a tendency to retaliate.

These patterns support our broader claim that retaliation is the particular purview of allies and reflect mechanisms and heuristics qualitatively distinct from both assistance and third-party enforcement.

Study 4 had two primary objectives: first, to examine another case of helping behavior and assess whether results would replicate the pattern observed in Study 3; second, to introduce an office scenario involving a mode of retaliation we expected participants to condemn.
We predicted that people might no longer favor retaliation for allies and might even rate third-party retaliation higher, as a disreputable act could undermine any obligation to engage in it.
Third parties could at least appear less self-interested.
If considered vindictive, the act might also shift appraisals of loyalty from high-minded commitment to mean-spirited favoritism.

text.text: The study findings provide strong evidence that people factor in both the identity of the retaliator and, more specifically, the relationship between retaliator and victim when evaluating decisions to retaliate-or not.
This evidence suggests retaliation is volatile and subject to circumstances outside the original provocation-and a valuable resource people believe must be used judiciously.
Further, the respective patterns in the retaliation and non-retaliation contexts were not simple inversions of one another.

In particular, both retaliating for allies and choosing not to retaliate for oneself operate as delicate reputational signals-especially as overall retaliation shifts from favorable or warranted to ambivalent.

To our knowledge, this is the first paper to directly compare evaluations of the actions of three central identities as they chose to engage in retaliation or abstain-especially as concerns valence, transparency, and loyalty, which proved a meaningful factor in our understanding of mechanism.
It also contributes to a relative gap in studies exploring decisions about whether or not to engage in retaliation in real-life conditions.

While a rising body of developing researchespecially involving economic games and third parties-has examined participant appraisals of retaliators, they have not often directly compared these three retaliator identities, especially in connection with overall approval of the retaliating act.
As represented most clearly by Study 2, judgments of overall retaliation coincided with different patterns among the identities we examined and their respective decisions.

For instance, in Study 2a, failure to retaliate for a friend was lowest, but this time (unlike in Study 1) failure to retaliate for a third party was rated nearly as blameworthy and more blameworthy in Study 2b.
Study 2b suggested that the less retaliation was endorsed, different patterns asserted themselves /became apparent.

These findings seemed to support the Integrity Hypothesis, part of which postulates that choosing not to retaliate for oneself (and for a friend) might represent a demonstration of magnanimity and/or transmit a message that this person has no need for retaliation.
For instance, imagine an example in which someone has overheard a co-worker making her the butt of a joke.
Retaliating might make her appear petty, whereas laughing it off may exhibit strength and self-assurance.
Likewise, choosing to retaliate and to refrain on behalf of a friend-both regarded relatively highly in Study 2b-could reflect tensions between loyalty and favoritism.
However, retaliating for an egregious wrong or even retaliating harshly also may be considered necessary-demonstrating strength-essentially "standing up" for oneself or others, as Study 4 suggested.
As Study 4 starkly exhibits, the mode and reception of retaliation may depend on the motivation-whether conscious or not-of the retaliator.
While people clearly condemned the behavior, they nonetheless registered a deterrence effect.

Both friend and third party were deemed likely to retaliate for a future offense and were also judged likely to be helpful-a combination that differs from the "helping" condition results, as do the patterns in Study 3.
In some circumstances, retaliation may serve a purpose when disproportionately severe from an outsider's-and even a retaliator's-perspective.
However, such gains may be short-term and also run the risk of alienating people who might regard the retaliation as excessive or frightening.

"Retaliation" may then seem more their jurisdiction and, therefore, more praiseworthy.

Indeed, much evidence has indicated that third parties-especially on an institutional level-have doubtlessly contributed to the maintaining of order in small ancient groups, as well as modern times (e.g., Boehm, 2019).

text.text: However, as perhaps our most tantalizing result, our studies demonstrate that such characteristics-impartiality in particular-may not always translate into praiseworthiness or endorsement for retaliation.
We argue that retaliation is fundamentally a partial mechanism, one that appears to be the purview of allies.
Afterall, when warranted, retaliation for friends prevailed as most praiseworthy.
Further, loyalty is a significant component in the mechanism underlying evaluations of retaliating-moderating and partially mediating the relationship between condition and praiseworthiness.
Consistent across studies, loyalty as a DV also tended to track praiseworthiness-and to distinguish among identities, even when praiseworthiness did not.
One possible reason is that people regard retaliation-even when likely to be condoned-as inherently costly; it therefore transmits a strong, relational signal of loyalty.

Indeed, retaliation for allies may thus constitute a separate mechanism from third-party retaliation, which likely has its own parameters-especially given that impartial third parties or institutions have not always been available or willing to intervene.

Such a possibility would coincide with Shinada & colleagues' 2004 results demonstrating that people are more intent on punishing members of their ingroup-vs. outgroup-presumably to provide order within their own community.

text.text: Our results provide some insight into this possible separate nature.
Undoubtedly, further research should how retaliation for allies and strangers may fundamentally differ.
Overarchingly, we set out to explore how identities and relationships affect how people evaluate retaliation.
Such a pursuit is significant because it is precisely onlookers-in addition to offenders-who stand to judge retaliation and those who engage in it by conferring benefits or administering costs.
In investigating retaliation-or the decision not to-for self, friend, and third party, we found that it can vary widely.
Yet distinct patterns emerged the more people endorsed or censured it.

Our findings have built on past research by suggesting that retaliation is a partial, valuable mechanism-likely the domain of allies-and is distinct from both third-party norm enforcement and straightforward assistance.
The initial studies were designed and conducted prior to the widespread adoption of preregistration practices.
For consistency, we chose not to preregister the later studies in this series.
Nonetheless, we clearly distinguish a priori hypotheses from exploratory analyses, and we outline the development of our predictions across studies.

text.text: Such results support findings indicating that while loyalty reliably tracks praiseworthiness to some degree, the two measurements do not always neatly coincide.

People may have regarded restoring stolen property, along with harsh words for the thief, as overwhelmingly praiseworthy and, partially for that reason, evaluations may have failed to differentiate among the identities on the retaliation side.

However, loyalty evaluations did significantly differ among the identities on the retaliation side, with friend highest, followed by third party-recall that self and third party differed in magnitude but not significance.

Interestingly, differences among the agents on the non-retaliation side largely coincided with the predictions of the Integrity Hypothesis: Failing a friend was most blameworthy and disloyal and abstaining on one's own behalf least blameworthy and most loyal.
